clinicalPearls: A rare recessive glycolytic defect that classically produces a muscle phenotype with exercise intolerance, cramps and exertional rhabdomyolysis
The muscle isoform (PGAM2) predominates in skeletal muscle, so myopathy is the dominant feature and haemolysis is variable when the erythrocyte enzyme is affected
Presents in some patients with pigmenturia (myoglobinuria) after vigorous exercise, akin to the muscle glycogenoses
When the red-cell enzyme is reduced, a chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia may accompany the muscle disease
A forearm ischaemic exercise test may show a subnormal rise in venous lactate, pointing to a glycolytic block
Diagnosis is confirmed by reduced enzyme activity on assay and PGAM2 mutation analysis
Management centres on avoiding strenuous exertion that triggers rhabdomyolysis, with supportive transfusion and folate if significant haemolysis is present
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphoglycerate mutase catalyses the interconversion of 3-phosphoglycerate and 2-phosphoglycerate in the ATP-generating lower half of glycolysis. Deficiency impedes glycolytic energy production; in skeletal muscle this manifests as exercise intolerance, cramps and exertional muscle breakdown, while in the red cell, which relies wholly on glycolysis for ATP, reduced activity can shorten cell survival and cause a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. The relative contribution of muscle and erythrocyte disease depends on which isoform and mutation are involved.
additionalInvestigations: Muscle or red-cell phosphoglycerate mutase enzyme assay
Forearm ischaemic exercise test measuring venous lactate and ammonia
Creatine kinase and myoglobin during and after exertion
Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film if haemolysis is suspected
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Molecular testing of the PGAM2 gene
redFlags: Exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of acute kidney injury
Recurrent severe muscle cramps limiting activity
Significant haemolytic anaemia when the erythrocyte enzyme is affected
Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection
reference.prognosis: The muscle disease is usually compatible with a normal lifespan provided provocative exertion is avoided; haemolysis, when present, is generally mild to moderate and well tolerated.
pitfalls: Attributing exertional symptoms to deconditioning rather than a metabolic myopathy
Omitting a forearm exercise test that would flag a glycolytic block
Not warning patients to avoid the strenuous exercise that provokes rhabdomyolysis
Overlooking a concurrent mild haemolytic anaemia
management: Avoid vigorous anaerobic exercise that provokes cramps and exertional rhabdomyolysis, and use gradual warm-up and paced activity
Treat episodes of myoglobinuria with prompt intravenous hydration and protect renal function, managing any acute kidney injury
Support coexisting haemolytic anaemia, where present, with folate supplementation and transfusion when needed
Monitor creatine kinase, renal function and haemolysis markers, checking urine myoglobin after exertion
Offer genetic counselling with PGAM2 testing of the family
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine and neuromuscular services
